reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: Lupus nephritis is renal involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus and is a major determinant of morbidity and long-term outcome in the disease
It can present across a spectrum from asymptomatic urinary abnormalities to nephrotic syndrome or rapidly progressive nephritic disease
Kidney biopsy is the cornerstone of assessment, classifying disease into histological classes that directly guide the intensity of treatment
The proliferative classes (particularly diffuse involvement) carry the greatest risk of progression and generally require intensive immunosuppression
Low complement levels and rising anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies often accompany active renal disease and can herald flares
Screening urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria at intervals is essential in all lupus patients because early nephritis is frequently silent

Treatment is divided into an induction phase to control active inflammation and a maintenance phase to prevent relapse, alongside general measures such as blood pressure control and reduction of proteinuria
Antiphospholipid antibodies can cause a thrombotic microangiopathy that contributes to renal injury independent of immune-complex nephritis
reference.pathophysiology: Lupus nephritis results from deposition of immune complexes and autoantibodies within the glomerulus, driving complement activation and inflammatory injury. Circulating and in-situ immune complexes, including those containing anti-DNA antibodies, localise in the mesangium, subendothelial, and subepithelial regions, and the site of deposition largely determines the clinical and histological pattern. Subendothelial and mesangial deposits provoke inflammatory, proliferative lesions with a nephritic picture, whereas predominantly subepithelial (membranous) deposits produce heavy proteinuria with less inflammation. Complement consumption, cytokine release, and recruitment of inflammatory cells damage the glomerular capillaries, and in severe forms crescents develop. Chronic activity leads to glomerulosclerosis, tubulointerstitial scarring, and progressive loss of function. Concurrent antiphospholipid antibodies may add a thrombotic microangiopathic component.
additionalDifferentials: Mixed connective tissue disease with renal involvement
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis with microscopy and quantification of proteinuria
Serum complement (C3 and C4) and anti-double-stranded DNA antibody titres
Full autoimmune panel including antinuclear and antiphospholipid antibodies
Kidney biopsy for histological class, activity, and chronicity indices
Serial renal function and blood pressure monitoring
Assessment for infection and other organ involvement before immunosuppression
redFlags: Rapidly rising creatinine with an active nephritic sediment suggesting proliferative or crescentic disease
Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema
Features of thrombotic microangiopathy such as haemolysis and thrombocytopenia
Signs of severe extrarenal lupus or infection complicating immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: Outcome has improved substantially with modern immunosuppression, but proliferative lupus nephritis still carries a meaningful risk of progression to end-stage kidney disease, especially with delayed treatment, high chronicity on biopsy, persistent proteinuria, or frequent relapses. Adherence, blood pressure control, and reduction of proteinuria strongly influence long-term renal survival.
pitfalls: Relying on serology alone without biopsy to determine the class and intensity of treatment
Missing silent early nephritis by not performing regular urinalysis in lupus patients
Overlooking antiphospholipid-related thrombotic microangiopathy as a cause of worsening function
Stopping maintenance therapy prematurely and precipitating a relapse
management: Biopsy-class-guided immunosuppression, with induction using glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide for proliferative disease
Add-on belimumab or the calcineurin inhibitor voclosporin to intensify induction and spare glucocorticoids
Maintenance immunosuppression with mycophenolate or azathioprine to prevent relapse
Background hydroxychloroquine in all patients, with renin-angiotensin system blockade to reduce proteinuria and control blood pressure
Monitor complement levels, anti-double-stranded DNA titres, urinalysis, quantified proteinuria and renal function to detect flares early
Treat rapidly progressive crescentic disease with pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone
Refer to nephrology and plan renal replacement therapy or transplantation for progression to end-stage kidney disease
General protection with vaccination, bone and cardiovascular risk reduction, and pregnancy planning given teratogenic agents
